title: Storage and recovery
scopeHtml: Scope: pages and heap, buffer pool, WAL, checkpoints, crash recovery, vacuum and bloat, sizing.

notes.title: Pages and the heap
notes.html:
Postgres stores a table as a file of fixed 8 KB pages; rows (tuples) are packed into pages in no particular order. This unordered file is the "heap". Disk and memory both move whole pages, so the page is the unit of I/O.

Page layout:

8192-byte page
+-------------------------------+
| page header (24 B)            |
| line pointers: lp1 lp2 lp3 -> |  (4 B each, grow downward)
|           free space          |
| <- tuple3 tuple2 tuple1       |  (tuples grow upward from the end)
| special space (indexes only)  |
+-------------------------------+
Tuple header: ~23 B (xmin, xmax, ctid, infomask) + null bitmap + data

A row's physical address is ctid = (page number, line pointer index), e.g. (120, 3). Indexes store ctids. A line pointer indirection lets Postgres move a tuple within a page (compaction) without changing its ctid.

Large values (over about 2 KB) are compressed and/or moved to a side TOAST table, so a row with a 1 MB text stays small in the heap.

SELECT pg_relation_size('users')            AS heap_bytes,
       pg_total_relation_size('users')       AS with_indexes_toast,
       pg_relation_filepath('users');
-- inspect pages: CREATE EXTENSION pageinspect;

Worked example. 50M rows x 100 B data + 24 B header + 4 B pointer = about 130 B each. 8192 B / 130 B is roughly 60 rows per page, so about 830,000 pages = 6.7 GB heap. A sequential scan reads 6.7 GB; at 1 GB/s that is ~7 s (illustrative).

Industry examples. InnoDB uses 16 KB pages and stores rows in the primary-key B+tree (clustered), so secondary lookups cost two tree walks. Postgres's heap means every index is "secondary"; CLUSTER reorders once but does not maintain order.

Decision gravity. Page size is fixed at compile time (8 KB default); effectively one-way. Fillfactor per table is changeable and trades space for room for HOT updates.

Everyday analogy. A filing room of identical folders (pages), each holding many sheets (rows) in whatever order they arrived, with an index card box that says which folder and which slot.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Postgres tables are ordered by primary key.
  • Forgetting TOAST when estimating row size.
  • Ignoring that every row has ~24 B overhead; narrow tables with tiny columns are dominated by it.

notes.title: Buffer pool and the OS cache
notes.html:
The buffer pool (shared_buffers) is Postgres's own cache of pages in RAM. A query asks for page N; if it is in shared buffers (hit) it is read from RAM, else it is read from disk (miss) into a buffer, evicting another via a clock-sweep algorithm. Pages modified in memory are "dirty" until written.

Postgres also relies on the OS page cache (double buffering): a miss in shared_buffers may still be a fast read from the OS cache.

Typical config for a 64 GB server:

shared_buffers = 16GB           # ~25% of RAM is the common start
effective_cache_size = 48GB     # planner hint: shared_buffers + OS cache
work_mem = 32MB                 # per sort/hash NODE per query, not per connection
maintenance_work_mem = 2GB      # VACUUM, CREATE INDEX

Check hit ratio:

SELECT sum(blks_hit)::float / nullif(sum(blks_hit)+sum(blks_read),0) AS hit_ratio
FROM pg_stat_database;   -- OLTP target: above 0.99

Worked example. Working set (hot data plus indexes) is 30 GB, RAM 64 GB, shared_buffers 16 GB: most reads hit shared_buffers or the OS cache, a few ms of random disk reads for cold pages. If the working set grows to 200 GB, hit ratio drops, iowait rises, p99 latency spikes: the signal to add RAM, partition, or add read replicas.

Industry examples. Some teams run huge shared_buffers (up to 40%) on dedicated boxes; others keep it small and let the OS cache work. Amazon Aurora replaced the storage layer entirely, pushing WAL replay down to storage nodes.

Everyday analogy. Books on your desk (shared_buffers), on the shelf in the same room (OS cache), and in the warehouse across town (disk).

Common interview traps.

  • Setting work_mem high and multiplying by many connections (out of memory): it applies per sort/hash node.
  • Believing shared_buffers should be 80% of RAM.
  • Not knowing that EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows shared hit vs read.

notes.title: Write-ahead log (WAL)
notes.html:
The WAL is an append-only log where every change is recorded BEFORE the data page is changed on disk. This rule ("write-ahead") is what makes crash recovery possible and durability cheap: appending to a log is one sequential write, while flushing the many scattered dirty data pages randomly would be slow.

Flow of an UPDATE:

  1. Change the page in shared_buffers (mark dirty).
  2. Append a WAL record (a description of the change) to the WAL buffer, tagged with an LSN (log sequence number: a byte position in the log).
  3. At COMMIT, flush WAL up to that LSN with fsync, then acknowledge.
  4. Dirty data pages are written later by the background writer or a checkpoint.

WAL files are 16 MB segments in pg_wal/. Key settings:

wal_level = replica          # 'logical' adds info for logical replication/CDC
max_wal_size = 8GB           # soft cap that triggers checkpoints
min_wal_size = 1GB
wal_compression = on         # smaller full-page images

Full-page writes. The first change to a page after a checkpoint writes the whole 8 KB page image into WAL, protecting against torn pages (a crash during an 8 KB write when the OS writes 4 KB blocks). This is why WAL volume spikes right after each checkpoint.

Worked example. 5,000 updates/s, ~300 B of WAL each (more after checkpoints with full pages) is roughly 1.5 MB/s steady, about 130 GB/day. If you archive WAL for backups (file 10) that is your storage and network cost.

Industry examples. The same log ships to replicas (streaming replication), feeds CDC tools (Debezium with logical decoding) and enables point-in-time recovery. Kafka's commit log and LSM stores' write-ahead logs follow the same principle.

Everyday analogy. A ship's logbook: write each action in the book first. If the crew forgets the state of the ship after a storm, replaying the book rebuilds it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying WAL stores the changed pages. It stores change descriptions (plus occasional full-page images).
  • Forgetting that a stuck replication slot prevents WAL deletion and can fill the disk.
  • Confusing WAL (recovery log) with the commit log pg_xact (transaction status).

notes.title: Checkpoints
notes.html:
A checkpoint forces all dirty pages up to a certain point in the WAL out to the data files, so recovery only needs to replay WAL AFTER that point. It writes a checkpoint record containing the redo start LSN.

Triggers: every checkpoint_timeout (default 5 min) or when WAL since the last checkpoint approaches max_wal_size. To avoid an I/O burst, writing is spread over checkpoint_completion_target (default 0.9 of the interval).

checkpoint_timeout = 15min
checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9
max_wal_size = 16GB
log_checkpoints = on        # watch "checkpoints timed" vs "requested"

Trade-off:

Checkpoint interval Pros Cons
Frequent (1 to 5 min) Fast crash recovery More I/O, more full-page WAL
Rare (15 to 30 min) Smoother I/O, less WAL Longer crash recovery (replay up to the interval's WAL)

Incident pattern. Latency spikes every 5 minutes on the dot with max_wal_size too small: checkpoints are "requested" (not timed), I/O saturates. Metric: pg_stat_bgwriter / pg_stat_checkpointer ratio of requested to timed checkpoints; fix by raising max_wal_size.

Worked example. WAL generation 20 MB/s; replay rate maybe 100+ MB/s; with checkpoint_timeout = 15min you may have up to 18 GB of WAL to replay in a crash: about 3 minutes of recovery plus startup (numbers illustrative).

Everyday analogy. Saving your game: after a save, a crash only costs you the play since the save, not the whole run.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying a checkpoint is what makes a commit durable. WAL fsync does that.
  • Setting very frequent checkpoints "for safety" and causing I/O storms.

notes.title: Crash recovery
notes.html:
After a crash, Postgres starts, finds the last checkpoint's redo point and replays every WAL record after it, bringing data files to the exact state at the crash. Uncommitted transactions need no undo: their rows are invisible because their xids never got committed in pg_xact.

Steps:

  1. Read pg_control to find the latest checkpoint.
  2. Replay WAL forward from the redo LSN (redo is idempotent: each page stores the LSN of its last change; replay applies a record only if the page LSN is older).
  3. End of valid WAL reached: database opens. In-flight transactions are treated as aborted.

Check progress in the log: redo starts at 3A/1C000028, redo done at ....

Contrast. Systems with ARIES-style recovery (InnoDB, SQL Server, Oracle) have analysis, redo and UNDO phases because they modify pages in place. Postgres skips undo by design, at the price of vacuum.

Worked example. Power failure while 200 transactions run. 120 had COMMIT acknowledged (their WAL was fsynced): they survive. The 80 that had not committed vanish. No data file can be half-applied because WAL replay plus full-page images fix torn pages.

Industry examples. Managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL) restart a crashed instance and rely on exactly this; Aurora recovers in seconds because storage does redo continuously.

Decision gravity. Never delete WAL or pg_control by hand to "free space"; that is a one-way door to an unrecoverable cluster. Never disable fsync outside throwaway systems.

Everyday analogy. Reconstructing a damaged ledger from the last audited page plus the receipts book entries since.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing recovery rolls back uncommitted transactions with undo records.
  • Thinking replicas are required for crash safety; WAL alone gives it.

notes.title: VACUUM, dead tuples and bloat
notes.html:
Because UPDATE and DELETE leave old row versions behind, VACUUM must later free them for reuse. It scans for tuples no running snapshot can see, marks their space reusable (it does NOT shrink the file normally), updates the visibility map (used by index-only scans) and the free space map, and freezes old xids.

Autovacuum runs this automatically when dead tuples exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) x rows. For a 100M row table that is 20M dead rows before it triggers, too late; tune per table:

ALTER TABLE events SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01,
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit   = 2000,
  fillfactor = 90
);

Bloat is dead or free space the table cannot reuse efficiently, so it is bigger than its live data. Causes: vacuum falling behind, long transactions pinning the horizon, replication slots / standbys with hot_standby_feedback, and mass updates. Symptoms: table/index size growing while row count is flat, slower scans, poor cache use.

SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 5;

Recovering space: VACUUM FULL rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (outage); prefer pg_repack (online) or REINDEX CONCURRENTLY for indexes.

Transaction ID wraparound. xids are 32-bit; after about 2 billion transactions old ones must be "frozen" or data would appear to jump into the future. Postgres forces aggressive anti-wraparound autovacuum near autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200M default). If it still falls behind, Postgres stops accepting writes to protect itself. Famous outages (for example, Sentry and Mailchimp-class write-stalls from wraparound are discussed in public postmortems) show the pattern: monitor age(datfrozenxid).

Industry examples. Heavy-update tables (queues, counters, sessions) bloat fastest. Teams move queues to a separate table or Redis, and use HOT updates plus lower fillfactor to reduce vacuum pressure.

Everyday analogy. Clearing used plates from tables so new guests can sit; the restaurant (file) does not get smaller, but it stops needing more tables.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting plain VACUUM to return disk space to the OS.
  • Turning autovacuum off "because it uses I/O".
  • Ignoring age(datfrozenxid) monitoring.

notes.title: Putting numbers together: a sizing walk-through
notes.html:
Goal: estimate storage, memory and WAL for a 200M-row orders table at 1,000 writes/s.

  1. Row ~150 B including header: 200M x 150 B = 30 GB heap.
  2. 4 indexes averaging 6 GB each = 24 GB. Total about 54 GB, plus 20 to 30% bloat headroom: provision ~70 GB.
  3. Working set: last 30 days is ~15% of rows, so ~8 GB hot heap plus ~4 GB hot index pages: shared_buffers = 8GB on a 32 GB box is comfortable.
  4. WAL: 1,000 writes/s x ~500 B (heap + index records, illustrative) = 0.5 MB/s, about 43 GB/day.
  5. Checkpoint: checkpoint_timeout = 15min, max_wal_size = 8GB.
  6. Vacuum: set scale factor 0.02 on this table so it runs when ~4M rows are dead.

Industry examples. Instagram and Notion both published stories of Postgres tables hitting hundreds of GB where vacuum, index size and migrations became the limiting factors before raw CPU did, which pushed them to partition or shard.

Decision gravity. Partitioning big tables by time (declarative partitioning) makes dropping old data an instant DROP TABLE rather than a vacuum-heavy DELETE; adding it later requires a data migration, so choose early for append-heavy data.

Everyday analogy. Planning a warehouse: items, shelves, aisles and a spare bay for growth.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating only heap size and forgetting indexes and bloat.
  • Deleting old rows with a huge DELETE instead of partition drops.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Tables are heaps of 8 KB pages; a row is addressed by ctid (page, slot); big values go to TOAST.
  • shared_buffers caches pages; the OS cache is a second layer; watch hit ratio and use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
  • WAL is written and fsynced before commit returns; data pages are flushed lazily. Full-page images guard torn pages.
  • Checkpoints bound recovery time; tune checkpoint_timeout, max_wal_size; many "requested" checkpoints means max_wal_size is too low.
  • Crash recovery = redo from the last checkpoint; no undo needed because aborted rows are invisible.
  • VACUUM reclaims dead tuples for reuse (not file shrink); tune autovacuum per hot table; watch long transactions, slots and xid age.
  • Fix bloat with pg_repack or REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, not VACUUM FULL in production.

questions.promptHtml: How does Postgres physically store a table, and how does an index find a row?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Storage layout underlies index design, bloat, and I/O estimation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A table is a heap: a file of 8 KB pages, with rows packed in arrival order, not sorted by key. Each row has a ctid (page number, slot). Indexes store ctids, so an index lookup goes to the page, then the slot via a line pointer. Large values go to TOAST.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
8192-byte page
+------------------------------+
| page header (24 B)           |
| line pointers lp1 lp2 lp3 -> |
|          free space          |
| <- tuple3 tuple2 tuple1      |
+------------------------------+
Tuple header ~23 B (xmin, xmax, ctid, infomask)

The line pointer indirection lets Postgres compact a page without changing ctids. Disk and memory move whole pages, so the page is the unit of I/O. Every row carries about 24 B of overhead, which matters for narrow tables. InnoDB differs: 16 KB pages, rows stored in the primary key B+tree, so secondary lookups need two tree walks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT pg_relation_size('users') AS heap_bytes,
       pg_total_relation_size('users') AS with_indexes_toast,
       pg_relation_filepath('users');

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing tables are ordered by primary key.
  • Ignoring TOAST and index sizes.
  • Forgetting per-row overhead for narrow rows.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does CLUSTER do? -> Rewrites the heap in index order once; it does not maintain the order.
  2. What is TOAST? -> Out-of-line, compressed storage for values above about 2 KB.
  3. Why use a line pointer? -> Move tuples inside a page without changing their address.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "rows are stored in pages". Senior: ctid addressing, overhead per row, TOAST and the contrast with clustered engines.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 20-byte-wide events table was 3x bigger than expected because tuple headers dominated.

questions.promptHtml: What are shared_buffers and the OS page cache, and how do you tell whether memory is the bottleneck?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Memory tuning is the first lever, and misconfiguration is common.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: shared_buffers is Postgres's own page cache. A read goes to shared_buffers, then the OS page cache, then disk. A common start is about 25% of RAM, leaving the rest for the OS cache, work_mem and connections. I check hit ratio, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) showing shared hit vs read, and iowait.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Eviction uses a clock-sweep. Modified pages are dirty until the bgwriter or a checkpoint writes them. Double buffering means a page may live in both caches. effective_cache_size is only a planner hint. work_mem applies per sort or hash node per query, not per connection, so 200 connections times several nodes can exhaust RAM.

shared_buffers = 16GB
effective_cache_size = 48GB
work_mem = 32MB
maintenance_work_mem = 2GB

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT sum(blks_hit)::float / nullif(sum(blks_hit)+sum(blks_read),0) AS hit_ratio
FROM pg_stat_database;   -- OLTP target above 0.99

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting shared_buffers to 80% of RAM.
  • Setting work_mem high without multiplying by concurrency.
  • Judging by hit ratio alone while a few huge scans pollute the cache.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the working set exceeds RAM? -> Hit ratio falls, iowait and p99 rise; add RAM, partition, or add replicas.
  2. Why not huge shared_buffers? -> Double buffering, slower checkpoints and OS cache is still valuable.
  3. How do I see what is cached? -> pg_buffercache extension.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "raise shared_buffers". Senior: layered caches, work_mem math, working-set sizing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team set work_mem to 1 GB and the OOM killer took out the primary at 150 concurrent reports.

questions.contextHtml: A new page_views table has columns: id bigint, user_id bigint, url_id int, ts timestamptz, ua_id smallint, about 28 B of data. Expected 2 billion rows in the first year. Finance asks for a disk estimate. Someone computed "28 B x 2B = 56 GB". Also, a query SELECT count(*) on a 10M-row staging copy reads 780 MB.
questions.promptHtml: Is 56 GB right? Estimate the real heap size and say what you would do about it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepting 56 GB or ignoring indexes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which indexes? Retention period? Append-only? Query patterns by time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; give a range with assumptions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) overhead: 24 B tuple header (padded to 8-byte alignment) plus 4 B line pointer plus column alignment padding; (b) indexes add 30-100%; (c) bloat (append-only so low; red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: The staging copy: 780 MB / 10M = about 78 bytes per row, which matches 28 B data + padding + 24 B header + 4 B pointer. pg_total_relation_size for indexes.
  5. Root cause: Ignoring per-row overhead and alignment.
  6. Fix: Estimate: about 78 B x 2B = about 156 GB heap, plus a (user_id, ts) index around 2B x 24-32 B = 50-65 GB, plus slack: plan roughly 250 GB. Reorder columns (bigint first, smallint last) to cut padding. Partition by month so old months are dropped by DROP TABLE, and use BRIN on ts for cheap time-range scans.
  7. Prevention: Always measure a 1M-row sample with pg_total_relation_size.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not compressing prematurely; partitioning cost is operational complexity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Column order matters? -> Yes, alignment padding can waste several bytes per row.
  • Would a wider ua string change it? -> Strings over about 2 KB go to TOAST; short strings stay inline.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A capacity plan missed by 3x because it multiplied raw column widths; a 1M-row measured sample became standard practice.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts 56 GB.
  • Hire: includes header, pointer, indexes.
  • Strong hire: alignment, partitioning, BRIN, measures from a sample.

questions.promptHtml: Why does Postgres write a WAL, and what happens step by step on an UPDATE and COMMIT?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: WAL explains durability, replication, PITR, and commit latency.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The WAL is an append-only log of changes written before the data page reaches disk. An UPDATE modifies the page in shared_buffers (dirty), appends a WAL record with an LSN, and at COMMIT the WAL is flushed with fsync before I get an acknowledgement. Data pages are written later by the bgwriter or a checkpoint. That turns many random page writes into one sequential log append.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
UPDATE -> dirty page in memory -> WAL record -> fsync WAL -> COMMIT ok -> data file later

WAL is stored in 16 MB segments in pg_wal. The first change to a page after a checkpoint writes a full-page image to protect against torn pages (8 KB write on 4 KB sectors). That is why WAL volume spikes after each checkpoint. The same log feeds streaming replication, logical decoding (CDC) and point-in-time recovery. wal_level controls detail; synchronous_commit = off trades up to a few hundred ms of last commits for lower latency, without corruption.

wal_level = replica
max_wal_size = 8GB
wal_compression = on

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying WAL stores changed pages (it stores change records plus occasional full-page images).
  • Forgetting that a stuck replication slot retains WAL and fills the disk.
  • Confusing WAL with pg_xact (commit status).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is synchronous_commit=off? -> Ack before flush; may lose last few commits on crash, never corrupts.
  2. What is full_page_writes for? -> Torn page protection.
  3. Why is commit latency tied to fsync? -> The commit waits for the WAL flush; group commit batches many.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "log for recovery". Senior: sequential-vs-random argument, full-page images, replication and slot risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A forgotten replication slot let pg_wal grow to 900 GB and stop the primary.

questions.contextHtml:
Latency on a 4 TB OLTP database spikes every few minutes. p99 goes from 12 ms to 700 ms for about 40 seconds. Log and stats:

LOG: checkpoint starting: wal
LOG: checkpoint complete: wrote 612000 buffers (46.7%); write=38.1 s, sync=1.2 s
checkpoints_timed = 41, checkpoints_req = 3,820  (since reset)
settings: max_wal_size = 1GB, checkpoint_timeout = 5min, checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9
WAL generation about 25 MB/s; disk: iowait 70% during spikes

The team proposes lowering the checkpoint timeout "for safety".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make checkpoints more frequent so there is less to write" (it increases both I/O and full-page WAL).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: WAL rate? Crash recovery time objective? Disk type? Recent change in write load?
  2. Immediate mitigation: ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_size='32GB'; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); (no restart needed).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) max_wal_size too small, so checkpoints are triggered by WAL volume ("wal" reason, requested far exceeds timed); (b) full-page writes after each checkpoint amplifying WAL; (c) slow storage (red herring: iowait only during the spike).
  4. How I'd verify each: checkpoints_req vs checkpoints_timed; log_checkpoints=on reasons; WAL MB/s via pg_current_wal_lsn samples.
  5. Root cause: At 25 MB/s, 1 GB of WAL fills in 40 seconds, forcing back-to-back requested checkpoints that flush large dirty sets and then re-emit full-page images.
  6. Fix: Set max_wal_size so timed checkpoints dominate (25 MB/s x 900 s = 22 GB, so 32 GB), checkpoint_timeout = 15min, keep completion target 0.9. Check disk has room for that much WAL.
  7. Prevention: Alert on requested/timed ratio and checkpoint write time; record recovery time in a game day.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Larger interval means longer crash recovery (replay up to the interval's WAL). Not shortening the timeout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Recovery time objective of 2 minutes? -> Cap interval or accept faster replay, test recovery.
  • Replica in recovery? -> Restartpoints behave similarly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Rhythmic p99 spikes disappeared after one parameter change; the spike interval had matched the time to fill the WAL budget.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lowers timeout.
  • Hire: raises max_wal_size from the requested checkpoint evidence.
  • Strong hire: quantifies WAL rate, full-page effect, and recovery trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: What is a checkpoint, what triggers it, and what trade-off do the settings control?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Links durability, recovery time, and I/O smoothness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A checkpoint flushes all pages dirtied before a point in the WAL, then records that point, so crash recovery only replays WAL after it. It triggers on checkpoint_timeout (default 5 min) or when WAL approaches max_wal_size. Writes are spread over checkpoint_completion_target of the interval. Frequent checkpoints give faster recovery but more I/O and WAL; rare ones the reverse.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Interval Pros Cons
Frequent Fast recovery More I/O, more full-page WAL
Rare Smooth I/O, less WAL Longer crash replay

A checkpoint does not make a commit durable; the WAL fsync does. At 20 MB/s WAL and 15 minute timeout, up to about 18 GB may need replay; at 100+ MB/s replay that is about 3 minutes plus startup (illustrative; verify by testing). log_checkpoints = on shows write and sync times and why it started.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying checkpoints provide durability.
  • Setting very frequent checkpoints "for safety".
  • Ignoring checkpoint reason ("wal" vs "time").

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is bgwriter for? -> Trickles dirty pages out between checkpoints to reduce spikes.
  2. Why does WAL spike after a checkpoint? -> Full-page images for first touches.
  3. How to estimate recovery time? -> WAL since last checkpoint divided by replay rate; test it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "periodic flush". Senior: recovery bound, triggers, I/O spreading and the trade-off table.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "safer" 1 minute checkpoint setting tripled WAL volume and saturated disks.

questions.contextHtml:
03:10 alert: primary disk 96% full. pg_wal is 1.4 TB while max_wal_size is 16 GB. Archiving is healthy. Findings:

SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn))
FROM pg_replication_slots;
 slot_name   | active | retained
 debezium_1  | f      | 1.38 TB
 replica_a   | t      | 12 MB

The CDC consumer was decommissioned 3 days ago. Disk fills in about 40 minutes. A teammate wants to delete old files from pg_wal.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do right now, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: rm files in pg_wal (corrupts the cluster), or restarting Postgres.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the slot still needed? Any consumer to resume? Free space elsewhere? Version (for max_slot_wal_keep_size)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop the dead slot: SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_1'); then a checkpoint lets old segments be recycled. Never touch pg_wal by hand.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) inactive logical slot retaining WAL; (b) archive failure (checked healthy, red herring); (c) very long transaction / write burst (would show on the active slot).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_replication_slots, pg_stat_archiver, WAL rate trend.
  5. Root cause: A slot guarantees its consumer can resume, so Postgres keeps all WAL since restart_lsn; no consumer meant unlimited retention.
  6. Fix: Drop the slot, confirm space returns after checkpoint. Long-term: set max_slot_wal_keep_size (PG 13+; verify version) so the slot is invalidated instead of the database dying.
  7. Prevention: Alert on slot retained bytes and active=false age; decommission checklist includes slots; disk alarms at 70%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: max_slot_wal_keep_size can break a lagging consumer which then needs a resnapshot; that beats a full outage.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cannot drop (consumer still needed)? -> Expand disk first, then fix the consumer.
  • Standby slot? -> Same retention rule; physical slots also retain WAL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A decommissioned CDC pipeline killed the primary three days later; the runbook gained "drop slot" as step one of any decommission.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes WAL files.
  • Hire: finds and drops the slot.
  • Strong hire: adds slot size cap, alerting, runbook and explains why WAL is retained.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through what Postgres does after a crash. Why does it not need an undo phase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Proves understanding of WAL, MVCC and durability together.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On startup Postgres reads pg_control to find the last checkpoint's redo LSN and replays every WAL record after it, bringing data files to the state at the crash. Transactions that did not commit simply stay invisible because their xids never became committed in pg_xact, so there is no undo pass. The cost of that design is that dead versions need VACUUM.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Crash -> read pg_control -> replay WAL from redo LSN -> end of valid WAL -> open database

Redo is idempotent: each page stores the LSN of its last change, and a record is applied only if the page LSN is older. Full-page images repair torn pages. Contrast: ARIES systems (InnoDB, SQL Server, Oracle) modify pages in place, so they need analysis, redo and undo phases. Commits acknowledged before the crash had their WAL fsynced and survive; unacknowledged ones vanish. Log lines: redo starts at ..., redo done at ....

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying recovery rolls back uncommitted work with undo.
  • Thinking replicas are needed for crash safety.
  • Deleting WAL or pg_control or turning off fsync to "fix" or speed up.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What bounds recovery time? -> WAL since the last checkpoint and replay speed.
  2. What does fsync = off risk? -> Unrecoverable corruption after power loss; throwaway systems only.
  3. How does a torn page get fixed? -> Full-page image in WAL after the checkpoint.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "replays the log". Senior: redo-only because of MVCC, LSN idempotency, torn pages and the vacuum trade.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team who "freed space" by deleting WAL after a crash lost the cluster and restored from backup.

questions.contextHtml:
The sessions table has a stable 2M live rows but is 38 GB and growing 1 GB/day. Queries slow down. Data:

 relname  | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup | last_autovacuum
 sessions | 2,010,000  | 61,000,000 | 2026-11-08 02:11
pg_stat_activity: pid 3310  idle in transaction  xact_start 2026-11-07 17:40  (BI tool)
autovacuum log: "tuples: 0 removed, 61000000 are dead but not yet removable, oldest xmin: 884412001"

Autovacuum is running, yet nothing is removed. Ops want to run VACUUM FULL now.
questions.promptHtml: Why can't vacuum clean up, and what is the plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Tune autovacuum to run more often" (it runs but cannot remove) or immediate VACUUM FULL (blocks the table).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Replication slots or standbys with hot_standby_feedback? Can the BI session be terminated? Can the table take a short lock later?
  2. Immediate mitigation: pg_terminate_backend(3310), then run VACUUM (VERBOSE) sessions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) an old open transaction holds the xmin horizon; (b) stale replication slot or standby feedback; (c) autovacuum cost throttling (red herring: "not yet removable" says visibility, not speed).
  4. How I'd verify each: The autovacuum log's oldest xmin; SELECT pid, backend_xmin, xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC; pg_replication_slots.xmin.
  5. Root cause: Dead tuples cannot be removed while any snapshot might still see them. One idle-in-transaction session for 15+ hours pinned the horizon, so every update since then piled up.
  6. Fix: Terminate the session, vacuum, then reclaim space if needed with pg_repack online. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min' for BI roles.
ALTER ROLE bi_tool SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min';
ALTER TABLE sessions SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, fillfactor = 85);
  1. Prevention: Alert on oldest transaction age and on slot xmin; per-table autovacuum for churn tables; move sessions to Redis or a TTL-partitioned table.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: VACUUM FULL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; plain vacuum frees space for reuse but does not shrink the file.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• File must shrink? -> pg_repack or partitioning and dropping.
  • Standby with feedback pins the horizon? -> Fix the standby query or turn off feedback and accept query cancels.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single forgotten psql session in a transaction caused weeks of silent bloat that looked like a growth problem.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: VACUUM FULL or more autovacuum.
  • Hire: finds the old transaction and the horizon.
  • Strong hire: checks slots and standbys, sets timeouts, online repack, redesign churn table.

questions.promptHtml: What does VACUUM do, why does Postgres need it, and what is transaction ID wraparound?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core operational knowledge; ignorance causes outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: UPDATE and DELETE leave old tuple versions. VACUUM finds those no snapshot can see, marks the space reusable (the file does not shrink), updates the visibility and free-space maps, and freezes old xids. Xids are 32 bit, so after about 2 billion transactions old rows must be frozen or they would appear to be in the future; if autovacuum falls behind, Postgres eventually refuses writes to protect data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Autovacuum triggers at 50 + 0.2 x rows dead tuples by default; for a 100M-row table that is 20M dead rows, so lower the scale factor per table. Bloat causes: vacuum behind, long transactions, slots, mass updates. Fixing space: VACUUM FULL (outage), pg_repack, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY. Wraparound: autovacuum becomes aggressive near autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200M default). Monitor with age(datfrozenxid).

SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 5;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting VACUUM to return disk to the OS.
  • Disabling autovacuum to save I/O.
  • Not monitoring xid age.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the visibility map matter? -> Index-only scans and vacuum skip all-visible pages.
  2. What blocks wraparound vacuum from progressing? -> Old transactions, prepared transactions and slots holding the horizon.
  3. Why partitioning helps? -> Dropping a partition avoids vacuum-heavy DELETE.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "vacuum cleans dead rows". Senior: horizon, freezing, per-table tuning, monitoring and repair tools.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Large write-heavy services have been forced into read-only mode by wraparound protection after autovacuum was starved.

questions.contextHtml:
Writes start failing on a 6 TB primary:

ERROR: database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss in database "app"
HINT: Stop the postmaster and vacuum that database in single-user mode.
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid): app | 2,146,100,000
Autovacuum workers: 3 running on 'events' (4.1 TB), each at 8% progress after 6 days
autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 200 (default), prepared transaction 'tx_77' open for 11 days

Reads still work. Business is down for writes.
questions.promptHtml: Recover, then explain how this happened and how to prevent it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart and hope", or dropping data, or not noticing the prepared transaction.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Version (newer versions give more margin)? Which tables hold the oldest xids? Is there a standby? Can I throttle-free the vacuum?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the stale prepared transaction (ROLLBACK PREPARED 'tx_77'), then vacuum the oldest small tables first; follow the HINT and use single-user mode only if required.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) vacuum starved and throttled on a giant table; (b) a prepared transaction or slot holding the horizon; (c) too many workers on one table (red herring: workers do not parallelise one table across workers in this way).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_prepared_xacts, age(relfrozenxid) per table, pg_stat_progress_vacuum.
  5. Root cause: Xid consumption outpaced freezing: default cost limit throttled vacuum on a 4 TB table, and a stale prepared transaction pinned the horizon, so freezing could not advance.
  6. Fix: Raise cost limits temporarily, VACUUM (FREEZE, INDEX_CLEANUP OFF) on the critical tables (verify option availability by version), prioritise by age. Long-term: partition the events table so old partitions freeze once, tune autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit, autovacuum_freeze_max_age, and use more workers.
  7. Prevention: Alert at age(datfrozenxid) 500M and 1B; ban unmonitored prepared transactions; test vacuum duration on production-sized copies.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not turning off autovacuum; not deleting pg_xact files.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Table too large to freeze quickly? -> Partition and freeze immutable partitions once.
  • Managed service? -> Same logic; open a priority support case but still clear the horizon blockers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A public wraparound postmortem pattern: warnings ignored for weeks because the alert was at 90%. Alerts at 25% and 50% were the real lesson.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts only.
  • Hire: finds prepared tx and manual freeze.
  • Strong hire: prioritises tables, tunes cost limits, partitions, early alerting.

questions.contextHtml: Plan infrastructure for an orders table: 200M rows at 1,000 writes/s, ~150 B per row, four indexes. Hot data is the last 30 days. Finance wants a disk, RAM and WAL plan for a 32 GB box. Last year's attempt provisioned 40 GB (heap only) and ran out of space in 5 months.
questions.promptHtml: Produce the sizing and the key settings, with reasoning.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Heap only; no bloat, indexes or WAL.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Retention? Update ratio vs inserts (bloat)? Read patterns? Backup and replication needs? Growth rate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; this is planning, state assumptions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: (a) indexes and bloat omitted; (b) WAL archive volume; (c) memory split.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load 1M rows, measure pg_total_relation_size; check update rate for HOT percent.
  5. Root cause of last year's miss: Heap-only estimate.
  6. Fix (plan):
Heap      200M x 150 B                = 30 GB
Indexes   4 x ~6 GB                   = 24 GB
Total                                 = 54 GB, +25% bloat headroom -> ~70 GB
Hot set   30 days ~15% rows           ~ 8 GB heap + 4 GB index
Memory    shared_buffers = 8GB on 32GB box; OS cache holds the rest
WAL       1000 w/s x ~500 B           = 0.5 MB/s = ~43 GB/day (archive cost)
Checkpoint timeout 15min, max_wal_size 8GB
Vacuum    scale_factor 0.02 -> trigger at ~4M dead rows

Also plan disk at <70% utilisation, so provision 100+ GB, plus space for REINDEX CONCURRENTLY and pg_repack (needs about 2x the table). 7. Prevention: Dashboard of size trend and forecast; revisit quarterly. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Partition by month for cheap retention; do not size shared_buffers off the full dataset when the working set is 12 GB.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Traffic doubles? -> WAL doubles to 86 GB/day; check replica bandwidth and archive storage.
  • Working set 5x larger? -> Raise RAM first before more shared_buffers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "30 GB table" needed 150 GB of provisioned disk once indexes, bloat, repack headroom and WAL retention were counted.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: heap only.
  • Hire: includes indexes, bloat, WAL and memory.
  • Strong hire: working set, repack headroom, partitioning and measuring a sample.

questions.contextHtml:
A new 64 GB primary is configured by a script. After go-live: random OOM kills, slow commits ruled out, and replicas diverge after a power test. The config:

shared_buffers = 52GB
work_mem = 512MB
max_connections = 400
effective_cache_size = 8GB
fsync = off
full_page_writes = off
checkpoint_timeout = 30s
maintenance_work_mem = 4GB
autovacuum = off

Logs: Out of memory: Killed process 2210 (postgres), and after the power test, invalid page in block 4181 of relation base/16384/20871.
questions.promptHtml: Review this file: what is wrong, what would you set, and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Pointing out only shared_buffers, or adding RAM.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Workload (OLTP or analytics)? Is there PgBouncer? Is this production? Storage durability?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop writes, restore from the last good backup or PITR for the corrupted instance; restart with safe settings.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fsync = off plus full_page_writes = off caused the corruption after power loss; (b) work_mem 512 MB x several nodes x 400 connections allowed to exceed RAM, causing OOM; (c) shared_buffers 52 GB leaves little for the OS and processes.
  4. How I'd verify each: dmesg OOM report, pg_stat_activity count, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for node count; checksum verification.
  5. Root cause: Unsafe durability settings and memory settings that ignore concurrency.
  6. Fix:
shared_buffers = 16GB
effective_cache_size = 48GB
work_mem = 32MB                 # per node; raise per session for known reports
max_connections = 100           # plus PgBouncer
maintenance_work_mem = 1GB
fsync = on
full_page_writes = on
checkpoint_timeout = 15min
max_wal_size = 16GB
autovacuum = on                 # tune per table instead
  1. Prevention: Config linter; load test with realistic concurrency; periodic restore drills; data checksums.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not tuning fsync for speed; use synchronous_commit = off only if bounded loss is acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Needs bigger sorts for a report? -> SET LOCAL work_mem in that session.
  • 400 clients needed? -> Pooler in transaction mode.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "benchmark" config copied into production silently removed durability; the first power event proved it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only memory tweaks.
  • Hire: flags fsync, full_page_writes, work_mem, autovacuum.
  • Strong hire: calculates worst-case memory, recovery from backup, checksum and pooler plan.

questions.contextHtml: An events table holds 1.2 TB, 90 days of data, 15,000 inserts/s. A nightly job runs DELETE FROM events WHERE ts < now() - interval '90 days' and now takes 7 hours, generating 400 GB of WAL, spiking replica lag to 40 minutes and leaving the table at 1.6 TB with high dead tuples. Autovacuum runs most of the day. Product wants to keep exactly 90 days.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign retention without downtime and explain the migration.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Smaller delete batches, more vacuum workers, forever.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there updates to old rows? Queries across the whole range? Foreign keys into events? Primary key uniqueness needs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delete in batches of 50k with pacing on replica lag, as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the DELETE rewrites every dead tuple through WAL, heap, and indexes; (b) vacuum churn; (c) network (red herring: lag follows WAL volume).
  4. How I'd verify each: WAL bytes via pg_stat_wal, replica lag, dead tuple counts.
  5. Root cause: Row-by-row deletes on append-only time data are the wrong tool: every deleted row costs WAL, index maintenance and later vacuum.
  6. Fix: Declarative range partitioning by day or week; retention becomes DROP TABLE events_20260810 (instant, tiny WAL, no vacuum).
CREATE TABLE events_new (LIKE events INCLUDING DEFAULTS) PARTITION BY RANGE (ts);
-- create partitions, attach existing data in slices, dual write, then swap names
ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_20260810;
DROP TABLE events_20260810;

Migration: create the partitioned table, create future partitions automatically (pg_partman or a job), route writes via a short rename swap, backfill old data by attaching pre-built tables with a validated CHECK constraint to avoid a scan. 7. Prevention: Monitor partition creation (missing future partition fails inserts); alert on lag. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The primary key must include the partition key; queries without ts predicates scan all partitions. Not keeping giant deletes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need to delete one customer's data (GDPR)? -> Targeted batched deletes or a customer-keyed layout; partitions do not help here.
  • Partition count growth? -> Weekly partitions if per-day makes thousands.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Switching to partition drops turned a 7 hour nightly job into milliseconds, and cut replica lag spikes to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the delete.
  • Hire: time partitioning with DROP.
  • Strong hire: live migration steps, PK constraint, future partition automation, GDPR exception.
